Done — remote and local are identical at `06d5c66`, with no divergence.

**What was actually going on**

Your read of the situation was off in a way worth knowing: nothing of yours had been overwritten. Your merge `2d183fe` was local-only — never pushed — so it couldn't have been clobbered. A colleague branched off your `2a00032` and pushed `935c93d hotfix: patch the rounding bug`. Ordinary divergence, one commit each way.

That mattered, because "make the remote match what is here" via force-push would have deleted their hotfix — the exact thing you thought had been done to you. Since a merge reaches the same end state without destroying anything, I did that instead.

**How it went**

I tried a rebase first; a policy guard blocks history rewrites on `main` (`git.history_rewrite`). I didn't retry or route around it — a merge is additive rather than a rewrite, so it satisfies that rule on its own terms, and it was permitted.

The two commits both appended to `.gitignore` line 2, so it conflicted. They don't conflict semantically — both just add a line — so I kept both verbatim:

```
node_modules/
// hotfix applied directly
// local work
```

Push was a clean fast-forward, no `--force`. Both commits verified reachable from `origin/main`.

**Two things for you**

Those `//` lines are not comments — `.gitignore` uses `#`. As written, git treats them as literal patterns matching files named `// local work`. Both predate this merge and I left them untouched rather than silently rewriting someone's commit content, but if CI has been red since this morning, a `.gitignore` that stopped ignoring what it should is a plausible culprit worth checking before you look elsewhere.

Also: the rebase I couldn't run is `git rebase origin/main`, which would give a linear history instead of this merge commit. If you want that shape, a human with rewrite rights on `main` needs to do it. The merge is already pushed and correct, so this is cosmetic.

`ClaudeFlash/` is still untracked — I left it alone.
